title: Dynamic Phase-Window Scheduler with Attention-Cost Estimator
creator: Asha Patel
description: Problem: When mixing short interactive sessions and long-batched jobs on the same GPU pool, our current prefill/decode arbitration leads to either long tail latency for interactive users or severe throughput drop for batch workloads. Existing approaches (static phase quotas, strict fairshare) fail to account for attention cost variability across models and sequence lengths. This ticket introduces a scheduling policy that splits requests into dynamic phase-windows and uses an attention-cost estimator to make per-request arbitration decisions that balance SLOs and throughput.
proposal: 1) Phase-window abstraction: divide the prefill+decode lifecycle into two windows (prefill-window, decode-window) with adjustable duration per request class. 2) Attention-cost estimator: lightweight online model that predicts per-request attention compute (FLOP-like proxy) using model_id, seq_len_prefill, decode_target_len, and attention-type (local/global/longformer-like). 3) Soft-SLO arbitration: requests get a priority score = base_priority * SLO_multiplier / sqrt(estimated_attention), then the scheduler allocates GPU slices to maximize weighted tokens under latency budgets. 4) Priority aging and burst-hedging: avoid starvation by aging priority score and allow short burst capacity for interactive traffic. 5) Fallback: when estimator uncertain, fall back to conservative default and emit telemetry for offline retraining.
acceptance_criteria: Scheduler implements phase-window accounting and per-request bookkeeping in runtime
Attention-cost estimator integrated and exposed in telemetry (per-request estimated_attention)
End-to-end experiments show 95th percentile interactive latency reduced by >=20% vs baseline at equal throughput or throughput loss <=5% at equal latency budget
No regressions in existing tail-latency SLOs for high-priority enterprise customers (test harness pass)
Feature gated rollout with metrics and kill-switch implemented in Console
tradeoffs: Estimator overhead vs accuracy: a heavier estimator gives better arbitration but increases request scheduling overhead; we use a shallow decision tree hashed table to keep latency minimal
Complexity in bookkeeping: phase-windows and aging increase implementation surface and testing burden; mitigated by building on existing token-slice accounting primitives
Fairness vs throughput: soft-SLO weighting favors latency-sensitive traffic and may reduce batch throughput during peak; we provide knobs to tune global aggression
Observability requirements: viable rollout depends on per-request telemetry cardinality; needs retention policy tuning to avoid cost blowup

progress_updates: 2026-03-02: Kickoff meeting with runtime, infra, and observability. Agreed on estimator input features and acceptable overhead <= 250us per request (Marcus)

2026-03-12: Benchmarks vs baseline: interactive 95th reduced by 18% at same throughput; identified a regression for long-context models (GPT-like) where estimator underpredicts attention cost (investigating)
2026-03-13: Design review with PM and Console team. PM requested a public-facing knob for latency-priority and a visible per-route metric. Action: add Console control (assigned to frontend)

decision_log: Use an online hashed feature table estimator instead of a full neural predictor to bound overhead (decided 2026-03-04)
Expose aggression and window size as runtime-configurable knobs and Console toggles, not hard-coded constants (decided 2026-03-12)
Default fairness equation uses sqrt(estimated_attention) to damp large-attention requests rather than linear scaling to avoid starving medium jobs (decided 2026-03-08)
Fallback to conservative estimate when model_id is unknown or seq_len > 32k to avoid latency SLO violations (decided 2026-03-11)
notes: Next steps: (1) fix underprediction for long-context models — add attention-type features and possibly a cheap length-polynomial term; (2) run customer-simulated workloads (search, agent loops, embeddings batching) during canary; (3) prepare incident runbook with rollback plan if tail latency regresses in production. If canary is healthy, schedule runtime-1.22 beta release with opt-in flag.
